moves.spoken: The opponent is walking into trouble — if the bishop gets taken, a capture on h5 leads to a forced mate in two. The whole ragged pawn adventure is backfiring.
The mate gets parried, but the pawn is still there for the taking — two pawns up now, and the enemy king dragged out into the open. It's hard to ask for more out of the first few moves.

Care is needed with the bishop's retreat: the opponent wants to capture on d4, and recapturing with the queen would leave the far-flung bishop hanging. So the bishop drops to e3, adding a second defender to d4 — now the pawn can be retaken by a pawn and the bishop kept.
Watch the developing move — the natural knight to f3 would be an outright blunder. The knight belongs on c3, because from there it threatens a leap to c5 that's very nearly mate.

That bishop has become a nuisance, so tuck it back to e2 and out of harm's way. It's a quiet, unspectacular square — but it's perfectly fine to park a piece passively when there's a concrete reason, and being two pawns up against an exposed king is reason enough.

Now an instructive question — which way to castle? Because the opponent has already stripped away the pawns in front of one wing, castling toward it would hand them a ready-made attack and justify the whole gambit. So the king goes the other way, castling long.

Before castling long, shoo the advanced knight away — but only as castling prep, since otherwise there'd be a fork winning a pawn. The knight itself isn't doing anything; removing it is purely about clearing the way to safety.

A guiding priority: it matters far less to wreck the opponent's pawns in general than to wreck the shelter around their king. Capturing here would only open a file that helps them attack, so it's declined.

The moment has come to open the centre — and the key is what not to do: resist locking it with a pawn push. Simply capture, prying the d-file open. Restraint over the tempting advance is the whole point.

The recapture weakens a key square, and now a tactic is waiting. Notice the relationship — the rook and queen stand on one line in an x-ray. Whenever that pattern appears, hunt for a discovery: if the front piece steps aside and a certain pawn were gone, the queen falls.

The move that makes both wishes come true at once is the knight capture on e5 — it removes the shielding pawn and unmasks the line in a single stroke. If it's recaptured, a discovered check crashes through.
And the discovered check on g5 ends it — not merely winning the queen but delivering mate in the process. Tactical awareness is exactly what makes these hidden shots easy to spot.

There's an even faster finish than grabbing the queen — a bishop check first, planting a piece on f7 to seal the king's flight square, and then the rook delivers mate. Blocking the escape before cashing in is the cleaner path.
